claim: Most bacteria use an indirect pathway to generate aminoacylated glutamine and/or asparagine tRNAs.
source: Most bacteria use an indirect pathway to generate aminoacylated glutamine and/or asparagine tRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about bacterial tRNA aminoacylation pathways.

claim: Clinical isolates of Mycobacterium tuberculosis with increased rates of error in gene translation (mistranslation) involving the indirect tRNA-aminoacylation pathway have increased tolerance to the first-line antibiotic rifampicin.
source: Clinical isolates of Mycobacterium tuberculosis with increased rates of error in gene translation (mistranslation) involving the indirect tRNA-aminoacylation pathway have increased tolerance to the first-line antibiotic rifampicin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Su et al., 2016; Javid et al., 2014) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: The aminoglycoside kasugamycin can specifically decrease mistranslation due to the indirect tRNA pathway.
source: Here, we identify that the aminoglycoside kasugamycin can specifically decrease mistranslation due to the indirect tRNA pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Kasugamycin but not the aminoglycoside streptomycin can limit emergence of rifampicin resistance in vitro.
source: Kasugamycin but not the aminoglycoside streptomycin, can limit emergence of rifampicin resistance in vitro
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Kasugamycin increases mycobacterial susceptibility to rifampicin both in vitro and in a murine model of infection.
source: Kasugamycin but not the aminoglycoside streptomycin, can limit emergence of rifampicin resistance in vitro and increases mycobacterial susceptibility to rifampicin both in vitro and in a murine model of infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Despite parenteral administration of kasugamycin being unable to achieve the in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration, kasugamycin alone was able to significantly restrict growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in mice.
source: Moreover, despite parenteral administration of kasugamycin being unable to achieve the in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration, kasugamycin alone was able to significantly restrict growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in mice.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and in vivo efficacy data (Figure 3C).

claim: Pharmacologically reducing mistranslation may be a novel mechanism for targeting bacterial adaptation.
source: These data suggest that pharmacologically reducing mistranslation may be a novel mechanism for targeting bacterial adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The long treatment duration of regimens for tuberculosis are thought in part to be due to phenotypic resistance (tolerance) of a subpopulation of genetically susceptible bacteria to antibiotic-mediated killing.
source: The long treatment duration of regimens for tuberculosis are thought in part to be due to phenotypic resistance (tolerance) of a subpopulation of genetically susceptible bacteria to antibiotic-mediated killing (Gold and Nathan, 2017; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Lewis, 2010; Wakamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased specific errors in gene translation – mistranslation – led to intracellular protein variants of the drug target of rifampicin, RpoB, which resulted in phenotypic resistance to rifampicin.
source: We proposed that in mycobacteria, increased specific errors in gene translation – mistranslation – led to intracellular protein variants of the drug target of rifampicin, RpoB, which resulted in phenotypic resistance to rifampicin (Javid et al., 2014; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a previously proposed mechanism supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Clinical isolates with mutations in the essential amidase gatCAB that mediates variation in cellular mistranslation rates had both increased mistranslation and rifampicin tolerance.
source: Clinical isolates with mutations in the essential amidase gatCAB that mediates variation in cellular mistranslation rates had both increased mistranslation and rifampicin tolerance, suggesting that this is a clinically relevant mode of antibiotic tolerance (Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Su et al., 2016).

claim: The indirect aminoacylation pathway is present in the majority of bacterial species (with the exception of some proteobacteria such as Escherichia coli), all archaea, some mitochondria and other organelles.
source: The indirect aminoacylation pathway is present in the majority of bacterial species (with the exception of some proteobacteria such as Escherichia coli), all archaea, some mitochondria and other organelles (Sheppard and Söll, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Bacteria lacking specific glutamine and/or asparagine tRNA synthetases instead utilize a non-discriminatory glutamyl- (asparaginyl) synthetase that forms misacylated Glu-tRNAGln and Asp-tRNAAsn aminoacyl complexes, respectively.
source: Bacteria lacking specific glutamine and/or asparagine tRNA synthetases instead utilize a non-discriminatory glutamyl- (asparaginyl) synthetase that forms misacylated Glu-tRNAGln and Asp-tRNAAsn aminoacyl complexes, respectively (Curnow et al., 1997; Rathnayake et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Misacylated complexes are specifically recognized by GatCAB and amidated to the cognate Gln-tRNAGln and Asn-tRNAAsn aminoacyl tRNAs, thereby preserving the fidelity of the genetic code.
source: These misacylated complexes are specifically recognized by GatCAB and amidated to the cognate Gln-tRNAGln and Asn-tRNAAsn aminoacyl tRNAs, thereby preserving the fidelity of the genetic code.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of GatCAB.

claim: In mycobacteria, strains with mutations in gatA causing partial loss of function are not only viable, but can be isolated from patient samples.
source: We recently identified that in mycobacteria, strains with mutations in gatA causing partial loss of function are not only viable, but can be isolated from patient samples (Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Strains with mutations in gatA have much higher rates of specific mistranslation – of glutamine to glutamate, and asparagine to aspartate.
source: These strains have much higher rates of specific mistranslation – of glutamine to glutamate, and asparagine to aspartate – since a proportion of misacylated Glu-tRNAGln and Asp-tRNAAsn complexes are not fully converted to the cognate aminoacyl forms before taking part in translation at the ribosome.
evidence: This is supported by previous work and mechanistic understanding.

claim: Wild-type mycobacteria flow-sorted for lower GatCAB expression had both higher mistranslation rates and rifampicin tolerance.
source: Wild-type mycobacteria flow-sorted for lower GatCAB expression had both higher mistranslation rates and rifampicin tolerance (Su et al., 2016), suggesting that targeting the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway may present a novel and attractive means for increasing mycobacterial rifampicin susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Kasugamycin at sub-inhibitory doses increased translational fidelity in both Mycobacterium smegmatis and pathogenic Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: Kasugamycin at sub-inhibitory doses (Supplementary file 1) increased translational fidelity in both the model organism Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) and pathogenic Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Kasugamycin decreased mistranslation in mycobacterial strains with mutated gatA that have extremely high misacylated-tRNA-mediated mistranslation due to partial loss of GatCAB function.
source: Importantly, kasugamycin decreased mistranslation in mycobacterial strains with mutated gatA that have extremely high misacylated-tRNA-mediated mistranslation due to partial loss of GatCAB function (Su et al., 2016) – Figure 1D, verifying that it was effective in increasing discrimination against translation of misacylated Glu-tRNAGln and Asp-tRNAAsn aminoacyl-tRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Kasugamycin decreased ribosomal misreading of mRNA in E. coli.
source: In addition to other reported activities in E. coli (Lange et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2016; Kaberdina et al., 2009; Moll and Bläsi, 2002), the aminoglycoside kasugamycin decreased ribosomal misreading of mRNA (van Buul et al., 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway is not present in E. coli.
source: but it was not known if it could also decrease errors due to translation of misacylated tRNAs, as the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway is not present in E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli.

claim: In an E. coli cell-free translation system spiked with a non-discriminatory aspartyl synthetase, kasugamycin can specifically decrease translational error from misacylated Asp-tRNAAsn in a dose-dependent manner.
source: An E. coli cell-free translation system spiked with a non-discriminatory aspartyl synthetase used in conjunction with the Nluc-GFP mistranslation reporter shows that kasugamycin can specifically decrease translational error from misacylated Asp-tRNAAsn in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Kasugamycin at 1500 µg/ml failed to significantly attenuate translation of canonical or leaderless transcripts in M. smegmatis.
source: The translation inhibitor chloramphenicol inhibited translation of both fluorescent proteins, but kasugamycin at 1500 µg/ml, more than 10 times higher concentrations than required to decrease mistranslation, did not significantly attenuate translation of either fluorescent protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Edeine and kasugamycin, but not chloramphenicol could decrease mistranslation rates.
source: Intriguingly, edeine and kasugamycin, but not chloramphenicol could decrease mistranslation rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that inhibition of 30S initiation might interfere with ribosomal discrimination of misacylated tRNAs by a yet to be characterized mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inhibition of 30S initiation might interfere with ribosomal discrimination of misacylated tRNAs by a yet to be characterized mechanism.
source: Intriguingly, edeine and kasugamycin, but not chloramphenicol could decrease mistranslation rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that inhibition of 30S initiation might interfere with ribosomal discrimination of misacylated tRNAs by a yet to be characterized mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Kasugamycin reduced mycobacterial rifampicin phenotypic resistance in wild-type mycobacterial strains.
source: In keeping with our hypothesis, kasugamycin reduced mycobacterial rifampicin phenotypic resistance in wild-type (Figure 2A,B) and high mistranslating gatA mutant mycobacterial strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Kasugamycin reduced mycobacterial rifampicin phenotypic resistance in high mistranslating gatA mutant mycobacterial strains.
source: In keeping with our hypothesis, kasugamycin reduced mycobacterial rifampicin phenotypic resistance in wild-type (Figure 2A,B) and high mistranslating gatA mutant mycobacterial strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Kasugamycin had no effect on mycobacterial growth in axenic culture.
source: Kasugamycin had no effect on mycobacterial growth, but addition to rifampicin significantly enhanced killing and sterilization of mycobacterial cultures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Addition of kasugamycin to rifampicin significantly enhanced killing and sterilization of mycobacterial cultures.
source: Kasugamycin had no effect on mycobacterial growth, but addition to rifampicin significantly enhanced killing and sterilization of mycobacterial cultures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The aminoglycoside streptomycin increases mistranslation.
source: The aminoglycoside streptomycin increases mistranslation (Leng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Plating of Msm on rifampicin-agar in the presence of sub-inhibitory concentrations of streptomycin increased the number of phenotypically-resistant colonies.
source: Plating of Msm on rifampicin-agar in the presence of sub-inhibitory concentrations of streptomycin increased the number of phenotypically-resistant colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plating Msm on rifampicin-agar with sub-inhibitory concentrations of edeine but not chloramphenicol, decreased the number of phenotypically resistant colonies.
source: Furthermore, in keeping with our observations with regard to 30S initiation inhibition and mistranslation, plating Msm on rifampicin-agar with sub-inhibitory concentrations of edeine but not chloramphenicol, decreased the number of phenotypically resistant colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming the link between reducing mistranslation rates and decreasing rifampicin tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A strain of M. smegmatis with a single point mutation in RpoB (Msm-RpoB-N434T) has lower tolerance to rifampicin since a critical rifampicin-binding residue could no longer be mistranslated via the indirect pathway.
source: This strain has lower tolerance to rifampicin since a critical rifampicin-binding residue could no longer be mistranslated via the indirect pathway (Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Msm-RpoB-N434T was less rifampicin tolerant than its parent strain, but kasugamycin was less potent at decreasing rifampicin tolerance further.
source: Msm-RpoB-N434T was less rifampicin tolerant than its parent strain, but kasugamycin was less potent at decreasing rifampicin tolerance further (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The major mechanism by which kasugamycin increased rifampicin susceptibility is by decreasing mistranslation-induced protein variants.
source: Since other reported activities of kasugamycin (Lange et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2016; Kaberdina et al., 2009) would not be affected by a single point mutation in the rpoB gene, we conclude that the major mechanism by which kasugamycin increased rifampicin susceptibility is by decreasing mistranslation-induced protein variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with the RpoB mutant strain.

claim: In E. coli, antibiotic resistance is preceded by tolerance.
source: In E. coli, antibiotic resistance is preceded by tolerance (Levin-Reisman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Kasugamycin but not streptomycin given alongside rifampicin pre-treatment significantly reduced the likelihood of resistance following high-dose rifampicin challenge.
source: Kasugamycin but not streptomycin given alongside rifampicin pre-treatment significantly reduced the likelihood of resistance following high-dose rifampicin challenge (Figure 2F), suggesting that kasugamycin may limit development of de novo resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both kasugamycin and streptomycin showed dose-dependent concentration-time profiles in plasma, with rapid clearance.
source: Both agents showed dose-dependent concentration-time profiles in plasma, with rapid clearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Administration of the maximum tolerated daily dose of kasugamycin – 400 mg/kg – resulted in a Cmax/EC(mistranslation)50 of ~2.5 and time over EC50 of 1 hr or only 4% of the dosing interval.
source: Administration of the maximum tolerated daily dose of kasugamycin – 400 mg/kg – resulted in a Cmax/EC(mistranslation)50 (peak plasma concentration divided by the half-maximal effective in vitro dose of kasugamycin in reducing mistranslation rates – Figure 1C) of ~2.5 and time over EC50 of 1 hr or only 4% of the dosing interval.
evidence: This is calculated from pharmacokinetic data and in vitro measurements.

claim: Co-administration of kasugamycin resulted in an astonishing 30-fold boosting of rifampicin killing of Mtb in mouse lungs.
source: Nevertheless, co-administration of kasugamycin resulted in an astonishing 30-fold boosting of rifampicin killing of Mtb in mouse lungs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Concomitant dosing of rifampicin and kasugamycin was poorly tolerated, even in the absence of tuberculosis.
source: However, concomitant dosing of rifampicin and kasugamycin was poorly tolerated, even in the absence of tuberculosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pre-treatment of axenic mycobacterial cultures with kasugamycin but not streptomycin decreased rifampicin tolerance, to a lesser degree.
source: In vitro, pre-treatment of axenic mycobacterial cultures with kasugamycin but not streptomycin decreased rifampicin tolerance, to a lesser degree (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sequential treatment with rifampicin and kasugamycin, but not streptomycin led to significantly enhanced killing of Mtb in mouse spleens but not lungs.
source: Sequential treatment with rifampicin and kasugamycin, but not streptomycin led to significantly enhanced killing of Mtb in mouse spleens but not lungs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which was not explained by differences in bulk-tissue PK (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and related supplementary figures.

claim: The differences in efficacy between lungs and spleens were not explained by differences in bulk-tissue PK.
source: Sequential treatment with rifampicin and kasugamycin, but not streptomycin led to significantly enhanced killing of Mtb in mouse spleens but not lungs (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 4), which was not explained by differences in bulk-tissue PK (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Generation of stochastic errors during gene translation – mistranslation – is more prevalent, and occurs at higher rates, than previously appreciated.
source: Generation of stochastic errors during gene translation – mistranslation – is more prevalent, and occurs at higher rates, than previously appreciated (Mohler and Ibba, 2017; Ribas de Pouplana et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Kasugamycin is unique among aminoglycosides in its ability to decrease translational error – all other aminoglycosides increase mistranslation.
source: Kasugamycin is unique among aminoglycosides in its ability to decrease translational error – all other aminoglycosides increase mistranslation (Leng et al., 2015; Ribas de Pouplana et al., 2014; van Buul et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ribosome has some proof-reading functionality beyond Watson-Crick base-pairing, limited to rejection of peptides formed from incorrect codon·anti-codon base-pairs.
source: It had been previously demonstrated that the ribosome has some proof-reading functionality beyond Watson-Crick base-pairing. This was limited to rejection of peptides formed from incorrect codon·anti-codon base-pairs (Zaher and Green, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Misacylated tRNAs would still form cognate codon·anti-codon pairs at the ribosome, and would therefore not be rejected by the ribosomal proof-reading mechanism.
source: Misacylated tRNAs would still form cognate codon·anti-codon pairs at the ribosome, and would therefore not be rejected by such a mechanism.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of misacylated tRNAs.

claim: Rejection of misacylated aminoacyl tRNA formation had previously been described at the aminoacyl synthetase stage or by discrimination by EF-Tu.
source: Rejection of misacylated aminoacyl tRNA formation had previously been described at the aminoacyl synthetase stage (Ibba and Söll, 1999), or by discrimination by EF-Tu (LaRiviere et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kasugamycin's binding to the E. coli ribosome is close to the A794 and G926 residues (E. coli numbering) of 16S rRNA.
source: Kasugamycin's binding to the E. coli ribosome is close to the A794 and G926 residues (E. coli numbering) of 16S rRNA (Schuwirth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural work.

claim: The A794 and G926 residues of 16S rRNA are universally conserved.
source: Given that these residues are universally conserved, it is likely that kasugamycin's binding to mycobacterial and other bacterial ribosomes is in a similar location.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosomal RNA conservation.

claim: Kasugamycin-bound ribosomes possess a hitherto unknown ability to discriminate against misacylated EF-Tu·aminoacyl-tRNA complexes.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that kasugamycin-bound ribosomes also possess a hitherto unknown ability to discriminate against misacylated EF-Tu·aminoacyl-tRNA complexes.
evidence: This is a novel conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The mechanism of discrimination against misacylated tRNAs potentially involves translation initiation, directly or indirectly.
source: Since edeine, another 30S initiation inhibitor, but not inhibitors of elongation (streptomycin) or peptide-bond formation (chloramphenicol) could also decrease mistranslation from misacylated tRNAs, this suggests a conserved mechanism, potentially involving translation initiation, directly or indirectly, in discrimination of physiologically misacylated tRNAs.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observations with different translation inhibitors.

claim: When kasugamycin and rifampicin were given daily, there was significant potentiation in mouse lungs after 2 weeks of treatment, but with significant toxicity.
source: When kasugamycin and rifampicin were given daily, there was significant potentiation in mouse lungs after 2 weeks of treatment (Figure 3A), but with significant toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and toxicity data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the alternate dosing schedule, potentiation was seen only in mouse spleens, not lungs.
source: However, in the better-tolerated alternate dosing schedule (Figure 3B), potentiation was seen only in mouse spleens, not lungs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Heterogeneity of drug distribution in either rifampicin or kasugamycin or both may explain the differences observed between lungs and spleens.
source: Even within a single organ/tissue, there can be significant heterogeneity in drug penetration and distribution (Prideaux et al., 2015), which we did not measure, and such heterogeneity of distribution in either rifampicin or kasugamycin or both may explain the differences observed.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences.

claim: A greater proportion of M. tuberculosis may be resident in macrophages in lungs compared with spleens.
source: Furthermore, a greater proportion of M. tuberculosis may be resident in macrophages in lungs compared with spleens, and aminoglycosides have poor intra-cellular penetration (Brezden et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation about aminoglycoside penetration.

claim: Aminoglycosides have poor intra-cellular penetration.
source: Furthermore, a greater proportion of M. tuberculosis may be resident in macrophages in lungs compared with spleens, and aminoglycosides have poor intra-cellular penetration (Brezden et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: At the maximum tolerated dose (400 mg/kg, once daily), the peak plasma concentration of kasugamycin (300 µg/ml) failed to reach the in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration of 400 µg/ml.
source: At the maximum tolerated dose (400 mg/kg, once daily), the peak plasma concentration of 300 µg/ml failed to reach the in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration of 400 µg/ml.
evidence: This is based on pharmacokinetic measurements and MIC determination.

claim: Most anti-tuberculous drugs require peak plasma concentrations orders of magnitude greater than in vitro MIC for measurable efficacy.
source: Most anti-tuberculous drugs require peak plasma concentrations orders of magnitude greater than in vitro MIC for measurable efficacy (Mitchison, 2012; Pasipanodya and Gumbo, 2011; Pasipanodya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The bacteriostatic kasugamycin given alone, administered intermittently (10 doses in 30 days) to infected mice, with a Cmax/MIC <1, and at plasma concentrations <25% of MIC for 99% of the dosing interval was able to restrict Mtb growth in vivo.
source: By contrast, the bacteriostatic kasugamycin given alone, administered intermittently (10 doses in 30 days) to infected mice, and with a Cmax/MIC <1, and at plasma concentrations <25% of MIC for 99% of the dosing interval was able to restrict Mtb growth in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the in vivo efficacy data and pharmacokinetic measurements.

claim: Streptomycin, a bactericidal aminoglycoside, given at far greater equivalent doses, had no effect on Mtb growth in vivo.
source: Streptomycin, a bactericidal aminoglycoside, given at far greater equivalent doses, had no effect.
evidence: This is supported by the in vivo efficacy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mycobacteria increase specific mistranslation rates under conditions such as nutrient limitation and low pH.
source: Mycobacteria increase specific mistranslation rates under conditions such as nutrient limitation and low pH (Javid et al., 2014), which mimic potential in vivo environments.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The efficacy of kasugamycin may not be as a conventional anti-microbial, but possibly by targeting bacterial adaptation to the host via reducing mistranslation.
source: These data suggest the efficacy of kasugamycin may not be as a conventional anti-microbial, but possibly by targeting bacterial adaptation to the host via reducing mistranslation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed efficacy despite poor pharmacokinetics.

claim: Most aminoglycosides inhibit translocation during protein synthesis, whereas kasugamycin inhibits translation initiation by blocking the mRNA channel in the small ribosomal subunit.
source: Most aminoglycosides inhibit translocation during protein synthesis, whereas kasugamycin inhibits translation initiation by blocking the mRNA channel in the small ribosomal subunit (Schluenzen et al., 2006; Schuwirth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: During 70S (leaderless) initiation, there is less steric hindrance of mRNA passage than in canonical initiation with kasugamycin bound to the ribosome.
source: The reported structures of kasugamycin bound to the ribosome suggest that during 70S (leaderless) initiation, there is less steric hindrance of mRNA passage than in canonical initiation (Schluenzen et al., 2006), potentially explaining why kasugamycin is permissive for translation of some, but not all (Schuwirth et al., 2006) leaderless transcripts (Kaberdina et al., 2009; Moll and Bläsi, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and functional studies.

claim: Kasugamycin is acting by reducing mistranslation generated by the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway with regard to potentiation of rifampicin in vitro.
source: With regard to potentiation of rifampicin in vitro, our data strongly suggest that kasugamycin is acting by reducing mistranslation generated by the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway, and hence protein variants that mediate rifampicin tolerance (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Most bacteria, with the notable exception of E. coli and a few other proteobacteria utilize the indirect tRNA pathway for synthesis of aminoacylated glutamine and/or asparagine tRNAs.
source: Since most bacteria, with the notable exception of E. coli and a few other proteobacteria utilize the indirect tRNA pathway for synthesis of aminoacylated glutamine and/or asparagine tRNAs (Curnow et al., 1997), targeting adaptive mistranslation (Ribas de Pouplana et al., 2014) may be a useful strategy in the treatment of diverse bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Targeting adaptive mistranslation may be a useful strategy in the treatment of diverse bacterial infections.
source: Since most bacteria, with the notable exception of E. coli and a few other proteobacteria utilize the indirect tRNA pathway for synthesis of aminoacylated glutamine and/or asparagine tRNAs (Curnow et al., 1997), targeting adaptive mistranslation (Ribas de Pouplana et al., 2014) may be a useful strategy in the treatment of diverse bacterial infections.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Kasugamycin (50 µg/ml) reduces asparagine-to-aspartate and glutamine-to-glutamate mistranslation in strain HWS.4 (M. smegmatis-gatA-V405D) with a specific defect in the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway.
source: (D) Kasugamycin (50 µg/ml) reduces asparagine-to-aspartate and glutamine-to-glutamate mistranslation – measured using a Renilla-FF luciferase dual reporter (see Materials and methods and Su et al., 2016) in a strain (HWS.4 – M. smegmatis-gatA-V405D) with a specific defect in the indirect tRNA aminoacylation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The D140N mutation in N-luc caused approximately 100-fold reduction in activity compared with the wild-type enzyme.
source: The D140N mutation in N-luc caused approximately 100-fold reduction in activity compared with the wild-type enzyme.
evidence: This is a characterization of the reporter system used in the study.

claim: Mistranslation specifically of aspartate (D) for asparagine (N) in a subset of newly translated polypeptides would result in regaining of wild-type N-luc activity.
source: Mistranslation specifically of aspartate (D) for asparagine (N) in a subset of newly translated polypeptides would result in regaining of wild-type N-luc activity.
evidence: This is the principle behind the gain-of-function reporter system.

claim: The Deinococcus radiodurans non-discriminatory aspartyl synthetase Dr AspRS2 is able to misacylate E. coli asparagine tRNA with aspartate.
source: The Deinococcus radiodurans non-discriminatory aspartyl synthetase Dr AspRS2 is able to misacylate E. coli asparagine tRNA with aspartate (Ruan et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The mycobacterial non-discriminatory enzyme does not recognize E. coli tRNA.
source: The Deinococcus radiodurans non-discriminatory aspartyl synthetase Dr AspRS2 is able to misacylate E. coli asparagine tRNA with aspartate (Ruan et al., 2008) (i.e. form Asp-tRNAAsn – the mycobacterial non-discriminatory enzyme does not recognize E. coli tRNA, not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments not shown.

claim: Addition of the non-discriminatory synthetase markedly increased mistranslation in the E. coli cell-free translation system.
source: Addition of the non-discriminatory synthetase markedly increased mistranslation, as measured by the Nano-luciferase-GFP gain-of-function reporter.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Kasugamycin at concentrations that did not decrease GFP signal was able to reduce mistranslation-induced Nluc signal in the E. coli cell-free system.
source: Kasugamycin, at concentrations that did not decrease GFP signal, was able to reduce mistranslation-induced Nluc signal (Figure 1E), confirming that kasugamycin could increase ribosomal discrimination of misacylated tRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Kasugamycin selectively inhibits translation of canonical but not leaderless transcripts in E. coli.
source: One of the activities of kasugamycin in E. coli is the inhibition of the translation of canonical mRNA transcripts (i.e. those with a 5' UTR including a Shine-Dalgarno sequence), but not leaderless transcripts lacking a 5' UTR (Kaberdina et al., 2009; Moll and Bläsi, 2002), although permissive translation of leaderless transcripts was not universal (Schuwirth et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mycobacteria have many annotated leaderless transcripts.
source: We wanted to test whether selective inhibition of translation of canonical but not leaderless transcripts with kasugamycin was evident in mycobacteria, especially since mycobacteria have many annotated leaderless transcripts (Shell et al., 2015; Cortes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Kasugamycin has been reported to generate novel 61S ribosomes in E. coli.
source: Kasugamycin has also been reported to generate novel 61S ribosomes in E. coli (Kaberdina et al., 2009), but our attempts to isolate such structures from M. smegmatis were unsuccessful (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature, but the authors could not replicate this in mycobacteria.

claim: Attempts to isolate 61S ribosomes from M. smegmatis were unsuccessful.
source: Kasugamycin has also been reported to generate novel 61S ribosomes in E. coli (Kaberdina et al., 2009), but our attempts to isolate such structures from M. smegmatis were unsuccessful (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from experiments not shown.

claim: Kasugamycin acts on the ribosome as an inhibitor of 30S initiation.

claim: The driver of aminoglycoside efficacy is Cmax/MIC (peak plasma concentration divided by in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration).
source: Since the driver of aminoglycoside efficacy is Cmax/MIC (peak plasma concentration divided by in vitro minimum inhibitory concentration) (Scaglione and Paraboni, 2006), we selected a streptomycin dose of 3 mg/kg, achieving a Cmax/MIC of 7, while the Cmax/MIC of kasugamycin was 0.8 (Supplementary file 1), thus avoiding underestimating streptomycin's activity.
